q: The technician says both water tanks are full. The panel shows this. What do you do before you sign?
a: Switch the selector to tank 2 and look into both fillers yourself
o: Sign — the gauge reads the tank not in use
Ask him to top up tank 1 and sign
Note 'gauge faulty' on the form and sign
why: A gauge reads the selected tank; a quarter-full tank 1 is the first thing to see — check both tanks at the filler before signing.

q: On the side deck you find three deck caps; the lettering has worn off. Your crew is already uncoiling the pontoon hose. What do you do?
a: Have the technician identify each cap and mark it before any hose goes in
o: Try each cap — water goes in the one that gurgles
Fill the aft one; water fillers are always aft
Fill the biggest cap; the water tank is the largest
why: Water in the diesel tank or the holding tank ends the week; caps are marked WATER, DIESEL, WASTE — if they are not, mark them.

q: You are filling the water tanks at the pontoon with the marina hose. How do you do it?
a: Run the hose clear first, then fill each tank until it overflows at the filler
o: Put the hose in, go to the shop and come back in an hour
Fill only the tank the selector is on; the other fills by itself
Fill through the galley tap so the pump stays primed
why: A hose that has lain in the sun holds stale water; fill to overflow, tank by tank, and stay with it.

q: Every tap is closed, yet the pressure pump keeps running. The technician says it is just priming. What do you do?
a: Switch the pump off and ask the base to find the leak before you leave
o: Leave it; a pump stops by itself once it finds pressure
Open a tap to let the air out and let it run on
Sign and switch it off at night to save the batteries
why: A pump that runs with the taps closed is pumping into a leak or from an empty tank — on a full tank, that water is going into the bilge.

q: Monday morning at anchor. Your crew report this. What do you do?
a: Run the engine for half an hour — the heater element only works on shore power
o: Switch on the inverter so the heater element can run
Open the hot tap and wait; the element takes an hour
Report it to the base as a broken water heater
why: The calorifier is heated by the engine's cooling water or by a 230 V element on shore power; at anchor only the engine heats it.

q: You are leaving the pontoon. The heads bowl is full of water and the pump lever is on 'wet'. What do you do?
a: Pump the bowl dry and set the lever to 'dry'
o: Leave it; the water keeps the smell down
Set the lever to 'dry' and leave the bowl full
Pump the bowl full so the seal stays wet at sea
why: A full bowl slops and can siphon when the boat heels; at sea the bowl is pumped dry and the lever left on dry.

q: A crew member reads the sign over the heads and asks whether the wipes she bought can go in. What do you answer?
a: No — only what has been eaten and a little paper; wipes go in the bin
o: Yes, if the packet says 'flushable' and you pump well
Yes, one at a time with plenty of pumping after it
Yes, in the electric heads but not in the manual one
why: Wipes do not break up; they block the pump and the holding tank, and the contract charges you for the unblocking.

q: Sunday afternoon in a bay. The crew are going ashore for lunch and the boat will be empty for three hours. This is how you leave it. What do you change?
a: Close the heads seacocks and the gas valve, and switch the pump off
o: Close the gas valve; the rest is fine for three hours
Switch the pump off; seacocks stay open to vent the heads
Close the seacocks; the pump must stay on for the fridge
why: An empty boat is left with seacocks shut, gas off at the bottle and the pressure pump off: nothing can flood or leak while nobody is aboard.

fig.title: Leaving the boat, 13:00
lines: Gas valve at the bottle: open

q: The technician shows you the holding-tank valve in this position, in the marina. What do you do?
a: Set it to 'tank' now and open it only when you are well offshore
o: Leave it; direct overboard saves pumping the tank out
Set it to 'tank' and never open it; the base pumps out
Leave it in the marina; switch to 'tank' once at sea
why: In harbour and in bays everything goes to the tank; the valve is opened only offshore, where the briefing allows discharge.

q: At check-in the holding tank reads this. The technician suggests you empty it at sea tomorrow. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to pump it out before you sign; a full tank is not an accepted boat
o: Sign and open the valve at the first bay tomorrow
Sign, and empty it over the side tonight after dark
Sign and note 'tank full' so the return check is fair
why: You take over a boat with an empty holding tank; discharging in a bay or a harbour is illegal, and the full tank is the base's job to fix.

q: The electric heads flush weakly and the bowl empties slowly. The technician says they are all like that. What do you do?
a: Write it on the check-in form and ask for it to be checked before you leave
o: Accept it; a slow flush is normal for a macerator
Sign, and use the forward heads all week
Sign; you will clear it yourself with vinegar
why: A weak flush is a blocked or tired pump that will fail mid-week; note every fault on the form and ask for the fix at the base.

fig.title: Electric heads, aft cabin
lines: Flush: a trickle, bowl empties in 30 s

q: The technician hands you this list and says the seacocks are 'all fine'. What do you ask for?
a: To be shown each one, turn it yourself, and have a bung tied beside each
o: To be shown the engine one; the others are small
To have the bungs counted in the tool bag
To have the list signed by him as checked
why: You need to know where every seacock is and that it turns; a bung tied to the fitting is found in the dark, one in a bag is not.

q: You lift the sole boards and find this. The technician says it is the fridge drain. What do you do?
a: Have it dried out and the fridge drain shown to you, then check it stays dry
o: Sponge it out yourself and sign; fresh water is harmless
Sign; the automatic pump will take it when it rises
Note 'fridge drain' on the form and sign
why: A dry bilge at check-in is your baseline: any water later is news; a fridge that drains to the bilge is a known source, but it is checked first.

q: The technician says the bilge pumping is 'automatic, you never need it'. How do you check the bilge pumps?
a: Lift the float until the pump runs, then find the handle and work the manual pump
o: Switch the electric pump to 'manual' on the panel and listen for it
Pour a bucket into the bilge and wait for the float to start it
Ask for the pumps' last service date to be written on the form
why: The float switch is tested by lifting it, the manual pump by pumping it — and its handle must be where you can find it with water over the sole.

fig.title: Bilge pumps
lines: Electric: float switch under the sole

q: The technician opens the gas locker and shows you this. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: A full spare bottle and the locker drain cleared
o: A full spare bottle; the drain can wait for the base
The drain cleared; you will buy a bottle in town
A note on the form that the locker holds water
why: Gas is heavier than air: the locker must drain overboard, not into the boat; and a half bottle with no spare runs out mid-week.

fig.title: Gas locker, cockpit
lines: Locker drain: blocked, 2 cm of water

q: Tuesday evening at anchor: there is a smell of gas in the galley. What do you do first?
a: Shut the valve at the bottle, ventilate, no flames or switches until the smell is gone
o: Switch on the fan and the lights to look for the leak at the stove
Light a burner to burn off the gas left in the pipe and hose
Pump the bilge and open the gas valve fully to flush the line
why: Gas sinks into the bilge: isolate at the bottle, ventilate, no sparks; then find the leak with soapy water on the joints.

fig.title: Galley, 19:30
lines: Smell of gas by the stove
Stove: off, gas valve at the bottle: open

q: In the galley you find this. The technician says the alarm 'kept going off, so we disconnected it'. What do you do?
a: Ask for it reconnected and tested before departure
o: Accept it; the solenoid switch is your safety
Sign and plug it in yourself later
Note it and rely on your nose for the week
why: A gas alarm that trips may be finding a real leak; it goes back on and is tested, and the leak is looked for, before you sign.

fig.title: Gas alarm
lines: Sensor: in the bilge under the stove
Solenoid switch at the stove: works

q: First evening in the marina, your crew start cooking. The stove swings on its gimbals as soon as a pan goes on. What do you tell them?
a: Lock the gimbals in harbour; free them only at sea so the pan stays level
o: Free the gimbals at all times; that is what they are for
Lock the gimbals at sea; free them in harbour
Wedge the stove with a cloth; the lock is for the oven
why: Gimbals keep the pan level when the boat heels; in a flat harbour the lock stops the stove tipping when someone leans on it.

q: After a night of rain the cockpit looks like this. What do you ask for before you leave the base?
a: The cockpit drains and the anchor-locker drain cleared and shown to run free
o: A bucket; you will bail the cockpit after rain
The scuppers checked; cockpit water drains over the sole
The anchor locker pumped out and the lid taped shut
why: A cockpit that does not drain fills in a sea; a blocked anchor-locker drain puts the water in the forepeak. Both are cleared at the base.

fig.title: Cockpit, Sunday 08:00
lines: Anchor locker: half full of water

q: You take over the catamaran with this. How do you plan the week's water?
a: Fill at every marina and make water only at sea, in clean water; 600 l will not last the week
o: Rely on the watermaker; run it every morning while in the marina
Fill once at the base; 600 l is plenty for 8 people for a week
Shower ashore only and never touch the watermaker all week
why: 600 l is under 11 l a day each for 8 people; a watermaker sucks oil and sewage in a harbour — it runs offshore in clean water.
